answer_text:
Let the 13th of each month be compared to the 13th of January.

In a **non-leap year**, the offsets (mod 7) from January 13 to the 13th of each month are:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Month} & \text{Offset from Jan 13 (mod 7)} \\
\hline
\text{Jan} & 0 \\
\text{Feb} & 31 \equiv 3 \\
\text{Mar} & 31+28 = 59 \equiv 3 \\
\text{Apr} & 90 \equiv 6 \\
\text{May} & 120 \equiv 1 \\
\text{Jun} & 151 \equiv 4 \\
\text{Jul} & 181 \equiv 6 \\
\text{Aug} & 212 \equiv 2 \\
\text{Sep} & 243 \equiv 5 \\
\text{Oct} & 273 \equiv 0 \\
\text{Nov} & 304 \equiv 3 \\
\text{Dec} & 334 \equiv 5
\end{array}
\]

So the offsets appear with frequencies:

\[
0:2,\quad 1:1,\quad 2:1,\quad 3:3,\quad 4:1,\quad 5:2,\quad 6:2
\]

The largest frequency is \(3\), occurring for offset \(3\). Therefore, the maximum number of Friday the 13ths in a non-leap year is

\[
3
\]

To achieve this, the 13th must be Friday exactly when the offset is \(3\). That means January 13 must be Tuesday, since

\[
\text{Tuesday} + 3 \text{ days} = \text{Friday}.
\]

January 10 is 3 days before January 13, so January 10 must be Saturday.

\[
\boxed{3\text{ and Saturday}}
\]
